summary: Reports on a prototype of the Source Address Validation Architecture (SAVA), built to stop attackers from sending packets with forged source addresses. It describes the implementation on an IPv6 network, the evaluation results, and lessons learned. It is an experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: Letter writers can lie about the return address. This paper tests a system that checks return addresses and reports how well it worked.

questions: what is source address validation architecture
how does sava prevent ip spoofing attacks
what is an authentication tag in source address validation
subtitle: A working prototype that validates IP source addresses to stop packet spoofing attacks across networks.

tldr.problem: IP packets are routed by destination address, not source address, making it easy for attackers to send packets with forged source addresses, enabling denial-of-service attacks and making it hard to trace traffic back to its origin.
tldr.mechanism: Implements a multi-layer source address validation architecture: checking at the access network (preventing a host from claiming another host's address), at the network edge (validating address prefixes), and between networks (using validation rules or authentication tags).
tldr.outcome: A prototype deployed on an operational IPv6 network across 12 universities demonstrated that multi-layer validation can prevent spoofing attacks and enable accurate network tracing, providing insights for future IETF standardization.

today: This is an Experimental document reporting on a prototype implementation and testbed deployment. The results provide insights for future IETF standardization of source address validation mechanisms.

sections.title: The Spoofing Problem
sections.content:
The Internet routes packets based on destination address. The source address is rarely checked during forwarding. This design decision made it trivially easy for attackers to spoof (forge) the source address of a packet, impersonating another host.

IP source address spoofing enables two categories of attacks: direct spoofing attacks that would be impossible without forged addresses, and spoofing-enhanced attacks that are more effective when the attacker hides their real address. Validating source addresses would make traceback accurate, improving network diagnosis, management, accounting, and security applications.

The Source Address Validation Architecture (SAVA) proposes checking that a packet's source address is legitimate at multiple points in the network, forming a multiple-fence solution that catches attacks even when some parts of the Internet are not protected.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad people send fake messages and hide where they come from. This checks whether the return address is real at several points.

sections.title: Three Levels of Validation
sections.content:
The SAVA architecture divides source address validation into three levels:

Access Network Validation ensures that a host in an access network (such as a WiFi or Ethernet network) cannot claim the IP address of another host on the same network segment. A SAVA Device at the network exit works with SAVA Agents inside the network to bind each host's MAC address and switch port to its assigned IP address. Only packets matching the binding are allowed through.

Intra-AS Validation happens at the edge router of an access network or autonomous system. The router checks that outgoing packets use source addresses that are legitimate for that network segment, typically using RFC 2827 ingress filtering or RFC 3704 methods.

Inter-AS Validation validates source addresses at the boundaries between different network operators (autonomous systems). When two SAVA-compliant networks exchange traffic, they validate that source addresses belong to the claimed source AS. This is divided into two sub-cases: neighboring ASes that exchange packets directly, and non-neighboring ASes separated by other networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Check at three points: at your home network (is this your computer?), at your ISP (is this someone in your ISP?), and between ISPs (is this from a real ISP we trust?).

sections.title: How Access Network Validation Works
sections.content:
The prototype implements two variants for access network validation. Variant A (binding-based) uses a protocol where the host requests an IP address from a management server. A switch port acts as a SAVA Agent, recording the host's MAC address and the port number. A SAVA Device at the network exit binds the IP address to the MAC address and port. Packets that do not match the binding are dropped. This variant requires switch upgrades but has good performance.

Variant B (signature-based) uses session keys derived from network access authentication. Each packet sent by the host is protected with a message authentication code computed using the session key and carried in an IPv6 extension header. The SAVA Device validates the signature to confirm the source address. This variant can be deployed without upgrading switches but has more processing overhead.

Both variants prevent hosts from claiming addresses they are not assigned, achieving host-level granularity of protection.
sections.plainLanguage: When you connect to the network, either the switch records your address and port, or you prove each message is from you by signing it.

sections.title: Inter-AS Validation and the Trust Alliance
sections.content:
For neighboring ASes (those that connect directly), SAVA uses AS-relation-based validation rules. Each AS maintains a table of which source address prefixes are valid on each incoming link, derived from the AS relationship (customer, peer, sibling, provider). When a packet arrives from a neighbor, the edge router filters it against this table.

For non-neighboring ASes, SAVA uses a trust alliance approach with authentication tags. Multiple ASes form a voluntary alliance. When a packet leaves one member AS destined for another member, the sending edge router adds a lightweight authentication tag (a shared random number) in an IPv6 extension header. The receiving AS validates and removes the tag. This provides mutual assurance: an attacker outside the alliance cannot forge a source address from inside the alliance because they would not have the correct authentication tag.

A central Registration Server maintains the alliance membership. Each member AS runs an AS Control Server that exchanges authentication tags with other members and configures the AS Border Routers that do the actual tagging and validation work.
sections.plainLanguage: Between connected networks, check the address against rules about what each network sends. Between separate networks, add a secret stamp on the packet so the other network knows it came from a trusted partner.

sections.title: The CNGI-CERNET2 Testbed
sections.content:
The SAVA prototype was implemented and tested on CNGI-CERNET2, a China Next Generation Internet backbone. The testbed was distributed across 12 universities connected to this operational IPv6-only network. Six universities deployed all three levels of SAVA (access, intra-AS, and inter-AS), while others deployed partial solutions.

The testbed included multiple test scenarios: normal operation (adding/removing tags, forwarding valid packets), dynamic changes (updating tags, new member joins, address space changes), and anti-spoofing tests (filtering forged addresses). Test results confirmed that fully-featured SAVA deployment prevents spoofed-source-address attacks and enables accurate traceback. However, the prototype identified deployment challenges: routers often handle IPv6 hop-by-hop options (used for the authentication tag) at limited rates, and managing authentication tag updates and refresh across many AS pairs adds complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: The researchers built it across 12 universities on a real IPv6 network and tested it. It worked, but it was slow and complicated to manage.

sections.title: Insights and Limitations
sections.content:
The SAVA testbed provided valuable insights into source address validation deployment. A key finding is that universal adoption is unlikely: deployment of local ingress filtering (RFC 2827) has always been incomplete, and expecting all networks to adopt SAVA is unrealistic. However, even partial deployment is worthwhile: a multiple-fence approach allows networks that do deploy SAVA to gain protection within the alliance, even if other parts of the Internet remain unprotected.

The document notes limitations in the prototype. The access network binding-based solution requires network upgrades. Both variants of inter-AS validation add overhead: authentication tag methods scale as O(N) per AS (linear in the number of alliance members) rather than O(1), and the hop-by-hop extension header creates MTU issues and router processing bottlenecks. Management of authentication tags (negotiation, refresh, invalidation timing) is complex.

The authors emphasize this is experimental research input, not a finished standard. The insights serve as a foundation for future IETF efforts in source address validation.
sections.plainLanguage: Not everyone will adopt it, but groups of networks that do trust each other can protect themselves. The main challenge is that routers are slow at handling the extra headers and managing the tags is complicated.
